->TO THE<-

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'D' featuring a figure in a robe, likely a saint or monk, seated amidst stylized acanthus-like leaves and floral patterns.</image-desc>

Those good people, being enlightened by the Spirit of God, have sought various manners, exercises, and paths to reach the highest perfection—that is, the highest love of God. Some have praised the path of <term>purgation</term> <note>from the Latin *purgatio*, referring to a spiritual cleansing or purification of the soul from sin</note> or of penance, so as to always mourn and keep their sinful failings before their eyes, washing and purifying themselves from all the impurity of sins with many tears of repentance. Others have believed they could reach this through detachment <note>original Dutch: "afghescheydenheydt", a central concept in mysticism referring to a spiritual withdrawal from worldly desires and distractions</note>, solitude, and the shunning of people, in order to thus preserve their hearts in peace,

<summary>This preface introduces the various spiritual paths—such as penance, purgation, and detachment—that devout individuals have historically used to seek the highest love of God.</summary>

# DR. JOHANNES TAULER,
->Divine teachings on the virtues, and the state of the highest perfection.<-

## CHAPTER I,
### Concerning the gravity of sins, and how we shall come to a loving union with God through true penance.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'P' decorated with intricate floral and leaf motifs surrounding a central vase-like form.</image-desc>

Do penance <note>original Latin: "Penitentiam agite"</note>, etc. Our faithful Lord Jesus Christ (who has sufficiently taught us the nearest way to eternal salvation through His holy life, commandments, and counsels in the Holy Gospel) began His holy preaching in this way, saying: Do penance, for the Kingdom of Heaven is drawing near to you. If we are ever to be saved, it is necessary above all else that we do penance, and never, during this life <note>original: "in desen tijdt," literally "in this time," referring to our temporal earthly existence.</note>, cease the improvement of our lives; for no one lives without sin. Now, it must be noted here that no one can perform true penance unless they first know how to rightly weigh the gravity <note>original: "swaerheyt," meaning the weight or seriousness.</note> of sins.

<summary>This page opens the first chapter of Tauler’s teachings, emphasizing that true penance—rooted in a realization of the weight of one's sins—is the essential first step toward salvation and union with God.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Tauler, penance, salvation, Kingdom of Heaven, sin, repentance, spiritual perfection, Jesus Christ</keywords>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>THE MARROW <note>original: "Het Merch," referring to the essential core or "marrow" of the doctrine.</note></header>
<meta>catchword: sin</meta>

A sinner does God such incomprehensibly great dishonor and disdain, and does himself such great, unmeasured, and ruinous harm; were it that he realized it, he would not, with deliberate intent, commit the very smallest sin, even to gain heaven and earth and all that is within them; indeed, he would rather allow himself to be put to a new death every day. For sin is a separation from God, a turning toward vain creatures, a stain upon the soul, a dying of the spirit, a snare of the enemy <note>original: "vyants," referring to the Devil</note>, a wasting of time, a robbery of God’s grace and of all virtues, and of eternal salvation. Sin is a distressing of the conscience, a darkening of the mind <note>original: "verstandts," meaning the intellect or faculty of understanding</note>, a perversion of the will, a restlessness of the heart, and an instability of the senses. Sin is an adoration of idols, a denial of the faith, an exaltation of the enemy, a sweet poison <note>original: "verghiffenisse." While this word usually means forgiveness, in this context of vices it is an archaic variant or error for "vergiftenisse," meaning poison—a common metaphor for the deceptive nature of sin.</note>, a beginning of damnation, a cause for further sins, a short joy, a long pain, an eternal shame; loved by the world, hated by God and by all good people. The gravity <note>original: "swaricheyt," meaning weight or seriousness</note> of sins cannot be expressed with any words; their harm is incomprehensible, their damage is insurmountable, and their pain is unbearable.

For from every sinner through the

...sin chooses and loves those base, perishable goods and its own pleasure <note>original: "wellust," referring to sensual or selfish gratification</note> above the highest good, which is God, and sets its own will above God’s will. By this, the sinner does God unspeakably great dishonor and contempt (to the same degree that God is better than such base pleasure and creatures <note>original: "creatuere," referring to any created thing as opposed to the Creator</note>); for which he also, by right, deserves nothing less than eternal hellish pain. Therefore, for true penance <term>penance: from the Dutch 'penitentie,' the spiritual practice of atonement for sins</term> it is necessary that the sinner, on account of such dishonor and contempt of God, fully acknowledge himself before God, humbly admit his guilt, and pray for mercy. He must praise and honor God from the bottom of his heart, and press himself down entirely below all people, and surrender himself into God’s most beloved will.

¶ And because he has sought wicked pleasure in creatures—which he should have sought in God alone—he must therefore mourn his sins with bitter remorse <note>original: "rouwe," meaning contrition or deep spiritual sorrow</note>. With true sorrow and a firm purpose to guard himself henceforth, he must admit his guilt in confession <note>original: "biechte"</note> before the priest in God’s stead (who has power to bind and to loose him <note>A reference to the biblical authority given to the apostles to forgive or withhold forgiveness of sins</note>) and receive penance according to the institutions of the Holy Church.

It is to be known here that this remorse should not come from a servile fear <note>original: "knechtelijcker vreesen," the fear of a servant or slave who obeys only to avoid punishment, rather than out of love</note> of hell

[to] such a wicked sinner out of His bottomless goodness / then he becomes ignited with such great remorse / that it seems to him that he can never have enough remorse / and prays not only that God forgive him his sins through His goodness / but also that He punish them in him through His justice / as it is more praiseworthy for him: for the more gracious God is to him / the more he weighs that which he has misdone against Him. Therefore he shall observe his sins / and lay them at the feet of our Lord / and lament them to Him with a bitter sorrow for his sins / and with a firm trust. The more heavily he deems the greatness of his sins / the more quickly God forgives them. For even though a mother might forget her own child / yet God cannot forget us / just as He says <note>A reference to the biblical verse Isaiah 49:15: "Can a mother forget the baby at her breast... Though she may forget, I will not forget you!"</note>.

His mercy is so great / that a piece of flax in a great fire is not burned so quickly / as God is ready to forgive the sinner his sins / when they are sorry to Him from the heart. For between the goodness of God and the repentant sinner / there is no time or delay <note>original: "middel," implying an intervening obstacle or step.</note>. Then a perfect faithfulness is formed between God and him / just as if the sin had never occurred. And God is so good that He shall never reproach him for that / which He has once entirely forgiven / and He shall not let the person suffer for it / as long as the person remains in a good life.

The foundation of true penance <term>penitence: from the Dutch 'penitentiën,' referring here to the inner transformation and remorse rather than just an external ritual</term> for sin / through which one comes closest to God / is that the person has a loving turning-toward God / and toward all virtues before God / and an eternal, firm turning-away from all that is against God / that same [never-]

[never]more to want to do [sin] / even if it meant dying the death. For to true penance belongs / that we weigh heavily the goodness of God / and His great faithfulness toward us / and suppress <note>original: 'verdrucken'—to humble or push down one's own ego</note> ourselves with great contempt / and hold our good works in low esteem. <page-num>8</page-num>

# THE MARROW

<meta>catchword: soul /</meta>

[to yield ourselves entirely] and recognize our unworthiness / that God has been and still is so mer- / ciful to us / and that we would not be able to / account for even this smallest benefit from God / what shall we then / do for the great unfaithfulness that we / have shown God in return for His great faithfulness? / Therefore we shall hold in low esteem whatever good / we do / even if we did as much as all creatures / could do / and we shall hold in high esteem / all that we lack. And we shall always / hold God in great honor and worthiness / and ourselves in great contempt and / unworthiness.

### CHAPTER IV.

->Concerning the humility,<-
->patience, and equanimity of a person dead to the self, and<-
->concerning some signs that he<-
->is not deceived.<-

Three things belong to a truly dead person <note>original: dooden mensch; this refers to the mystical concept of "dying to the self" or ego-death to live in God</note>. The first is that he is sunk into the earth / the second is that he may be trodden upon with feet until the Last Day / the third is that his body becomes nothing. By these three points one may recognize a divinely dead person. Firstly, a divinely dead person sinks beneath God / and beneath all people in such bottomless **humility** <term>ootmoedicheyt: the core virtue of spiritual lowliness and submission</term> so deeply / that he never again raises himself up in his spirit against any person. And he considers himself the lowliest person living here / so that all people are better and holier before God than he is. The second is / he suffers with patient **equanimity** <term>ghelatentheyt: a state of total resignation or "letting be," where one accepts all things as coming from God's will</term> / that one treads upon him until the Last Day / that is, until the last day of his life he shall endure / all adversity / all shame and contempt / all pain and suffering / however they may come upon him from God or from creatures / whether right or wrong happens to him / he shall not answer-
<meta>The word "beantwoorden" (to answer/respond) is split by the page break; "woorden" will begin the next page.</meta>

<summary>This page outlines the three hallmarks of a person who has achieved spiritual "death to the self": profound humility, the patient endurance of mistreatment, and total self-abnegation.</summary>
<keywords>humility, equanimity, self-mortification, patience, spiritual death, resignation</keywords>

Up to this point, we have spoken of the <term>resignation<note>original: "ghelaetenheyt." Refers to pure spiritual essences or angelic beings that exist apart from matter.</note></term>. It does not shine within time but sleeps in **eternity**, sinking away from itself entirely, and stripping away—starkly and clearly—all that it is capable of, all that it is, and all that it can know, love, possess, behold, or use. If a person flees an entire kingdom or the wide world, yet kept himself <note>meaning his own ego or "selfhood"</note>, then he has not left much behind. But he who leaves himself utterly—whatever he then retains, be it riches, honor, or whatever else he must keep—he has left all things behind. For he can use all things for the honor of God and for his own strict necessity <note>original: "scherpen nootdruft," meaning only what is absolutely essential for survival.</note>, like one to whom they are lent and entrusted; like a servant who distributes what is left over to the poor, and does not possess things with disordered love <term>disordered love<note>original: "ongheordineerder liefden." A concept where one’s affections are out of balance, loving created things for their own sake rather than as tools to love God.</note></term>. 

And when he sees that another needs the goods more than he does, it seems to him that they belong more to the other than to himself. For he is fundamentally turned away from all temporal goods and dealings, and is more inclined toward contempt <note>Choosing to be lowly or disregarded by the world.</note> than toward honor, and toward being submissive than toward being a leader.

See, here we shall hide <note>original: "herborghen," meaning to take shelter or be hidden away for safety.</note> ourselves in his Divine nature, so that we remain unmoved in our desolation, helping ourselves with no things or creatures, but only with the words that Christ spoke: *Thy will be done.* <note>original Latin: "Fiat voluntas tua."</note> Your will be done and fulfilled in me. God is such an ordered being <term>gheschickte wesen: a being that is properly disposed or perfectly structured; here it refers to the transcendent nature of God which defies human categorization.</term> that one knows him no better than through "nothing." How through "nothing"? That one sets aside every means—not only despising the world and possessing virtues, but I must let go of the very mental image <note>original: "beeldinghe," referring to the concepts or intellectual "pictures" we form of holy things.</note> of the virtues if I am to see God without mediation <term>sonder middel: a mystical term meaning "without means" or "immediately," referring to a direct union with God that bypasses all thoughts, symbols, or created things.</term>. Not in such a way that I despise the virtues, but that virtue shall become essential <term>weselijck: relating to the "wesen" or essence; meaning the virtue becomes a part of the soul's very nature rather than a forced effort.</term> in me, and flow out of me and be practiced without my [conscious] effort.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## Regarding internal detachment, by which we remain united with God in all works and places.

He who wishes to lead a truly detached life must dwell in the city of Jerusalem—that is, in peace <note>The name Jerusalem was traditionally interpreted in mystical theology as "Vision of Peace."</note>—and must be without the punishment of mortal sins, and free from all disordered inclination toward creatures <note>In this context, "creatures" refers to any created thing, person, or worldly desire, as opposed to the Creator.</note>, whether of love or of sorrow. He must lift up his mind <term>moet: the inner spirit, disposition, or higher mind.</term> to God without hindrance, and constantly observe God, and satisfy His movements and promptings, and be always inclined toward God. For a detached life is more internal than external. And just as an imperfect person must flee external things if he is to turn himself entirely to God—and that not without great pain and labor (for the things we possess with [worldly] love remind us of themselves whether we wish it or not)—so the perfect person does not need to flee external things. For he possesses nothing with disordered love, and his inward turning to God is ready and easy for him through love, constant practice, and the observation of God, so that he [himself]...

<summary>This chapter explains that true spiritual detachment is an internal state of peace ("Jerusalem") rather than a mere avoidance of the physical world. It distinguishes between the "imperfect" person who must struggle to avoid distractions and the "perfect" person whose internal union with God is so stable that external things no longer pull them away.</summary>

<keywords>internal detachment, Jerusalem, peace, disordered love, creatures, spiritual practice, union with God, mindfulness</keywords>

And although it is not possible for us to always remain stretched out <note>The Dutch *uyt ghereckt* suggests a state of total spiritual tension or focused extension toward the Divine.</note> in God as long as we are in time <note>A common mystical phrase meaning "as long as we are living in this temporal, mortal world."</note>, nevertheless, as soon as a good person becomes aware that he has turned toward useless things, he easily turns away from them with great indignation toward himself for being so unsteady. And because he views those things without attachment, he can turn away from them without labor. For he is more inclined toward the **inward turn** <term>inkeer: the meditative practice of withdrawing the senses and focusing the soul entirely on the presence of God within.</term> than toward the **outward turn** <term>uytkeer: focusing one's attention on external, worldly matters.</term>.

One person is also quieter by nature than another, but for that reason, he is not holier. But he who has more divine love, and observes God better, and fulfills that observation, and fights chivalrously for God, and dies more to his own faults <note>The original *afsterft* refers to the process of mortification, or "killing off" one's ego and sinful inclinations.</note>—he is the holiest. For this person has a great desire for God and a burning love, and he weighs small faults so heavily that he can hardly endure himself out of great sorrow and self-abasement. Therefore, he guards himself with great diligence against all faults, purely for the glory of God. For the slightest thing that is against God causes him more pain than all the harm that could ever befall him personally. And the more he exercises himself in love, the holier he becomes.

## THE XVII. CHAPTER.

### How a good person, united with God's will, is capable of all things, and concerning inward consolation and desolation.

A person should not take things too much to heart, nor grieve too greatly, nor consider himself far from God, so long as he finds himself in possession of a good will. For virtue and all goodness consist in the will. One cannot fail, provided that you have a righteous and true will. If you wish to have <term>humility: ootmoedicheyt, a central virtue in this tradition involving the recognition of one's own nothingness before God.</term>, love, and other virtues—if you desire this powerfully and with your whole will—then you already possess them. And neither God nor any <term>creature: any created being or object, as opposed to the Creator.</term> can take that from you, so long as your will is a righteous, Divine will. 

A Divine will is this: that everything one desires, one desires purely for the glory of God. For our natural will does not have this by its own nature; and nowhere can the Divine will be more clearly recognized than when a person intends the glory of God alone. Nothing can overcome this will—neither death, nor life, nor the devil, nor any created thing. One must not say—

## CHAPTER XXIII.

### How we shall become one with Christ, and walk in Heaven.

Saint Paul says: "I know a man in Christ." This word is understood by few people—what it means to be "one in Christ." To achieve this, there must be a state of abandonment <term>abandonment: "ghelaetentheydt," the mystical practice of surrendering one's own will and ego</term> regarding everything that is not "the One." This applies to whatever and in what manner any thing has any other status or condition than in Christ, whether it concerns people outwardly or inwardly. Those who dwell in eternal life are so much at one, that each of them, from the very ground <note>original: "gronde"; referring to the "ground of the soul," the deepest part of the human spirit where it meets the divine</note> of their being, rejoices as much in the joy of another through goodwill as they do in their own happiness. And every person who is the lowest would not wish to be the highest. Their will is so perfectly conformed to God’s will. In the same way, our will should also be one with God’s will. In God there is no distinction between Jews or Gentiles <note>original: "Heydenen"; literally "heathens," but referring here to the Pauline distinction between Jews and non-Jews</note>. But while Saint Paul was still on earth, he might have been more intimate with one person than another, and might have loved one more than another, but that was not in the slightest bit except in Christ. On the contrary, in all ways, if he found people in Christ, or if he were to bring them into it...

<summary>This chapter explains the mystical union with Christ through "abandonment" of the self, illustrating how souls in heaven share perfectly in each other's joy by aligning their wills with God's. It uses Saint Paul as an example of one who loved others only through their shared connection in Christ.</summary>
<keywords>Saint Paul, mystical union, abandonment, ghelaetentheydt, ground of the soul, divine will, equality in heaven, Christian community</keywords>

# CHAPTER XXX.

## Many reasons why we shall love our enemy from the heart.

Our dear Lord Jesus Christ allowed Judas, his mortal enemy, to walk with him for seven reasons. The first is: he wanted to have before his human eyes at all times that man who would deliver him to death, so that his Passion <term>Passion; from the Latin 'passio', meaning suffering. In this context, it refers specifically to the physical and spiritual suffering of Christ leading up to the crucifixion.</term> and martyrdom would be renewed for him at all times. For just as he well knew his Passion in his Divine eternal wisdom, so he also wanted never to forget his pains before his human eyes; therefore it was always renewed for him in time <note>The author suggests that while Christ knew his fate eternally as God, he chose to keep the physical reminder of his betrayer present to experience the weight of that suffering within human time.</note>. The second is: he wanted to prove with deeds what he taught us with words: to love enemies as friends. The third is: that he taught us thereby that we have no cause to avoid love; we can always practice ourselves well in it. The fourth is: that he wanted to give an example to all the world, which by its adopted wickedness is inclined to destroy the good. For he knew that after his death followers of Judas would arise; so that the world would not then destroy the good with the evil, he wanted...

<summary>This page explores the theological reasons why Christ tolerated Judas, emphasizing that Christ's proximity to his betrayer was a deliberate act to keep his upcoming sacrifice at the forefront of his human experience and to model perfect love for one's enemies.</summary>

Christ also suffered <note>original: "lijden"; in this context, it means to endure or tolerate the presence of someone, similar to the archaic English use in "suffer the little children."</note> the wicked in his company. The fifth is: if a Judas should arise among his true friends, they should not despair or lose heart because of it, but they should lovingly suffer him to be among them, just as Christ suffered him. 

The sixth is: Because the dear Son of God had come into the world out of eternal love and had brought us an exercise <note>original: "oeffeninghe"; a spiritual practice or a living demonstration.</note> of his bottomless love and mercy, he also wanted to prove this to Judas, to whom he did good just as he did to his chosen friends. He did this so that he would give him no cause for the deed and the evil that he [Judas] took upon himself out of his own wicked will. For He knew in eternity that Judas would deliver him to death. 

The seventh reason is: although God knew from eternity that Judas would betray him and take that great wickedness upon himself of his own free will, Christ had not chosen him for that wickedness. For otherwise God would have been a cause of the evil—which was not the case—but Judas was himself the cause of the wickedness. Therefore, He let him walk with Him as His chosen one, so that He might draw him not toward despair, but to trust in His mercy. And note this by the words He spoke that evening: "Friend..." <note>A reference to Matthew 26:50, where Jesus addresses Judas as "Friend" in the Garden of Gethsemane during the betrayal.</note>

It is a question: whether one may give leave to <term>images</term> <note>original: "beelden" – in the tradition of Rhineland mysticism, "images" refers to mental concepts, sensory perceptions, or theological ideas that the mind uses to understand God.</note> and cling to God with a naked mind? Answer: One may give leave to images in two ways: foolishly and also harmfully. That is, if I give leave to all good images before I have gained knowledge of them, then I have given leave to them foolishly and harmfully. Why? Because by doing so, the truth—which every good image would have signified for me—escapes me. Which are the most useful images that a person can have? The first is that a person rightly acknowledges, with heartfelt remorse and a complete turning-away, his previous sinful life. The second is that he learns to acknowledge the life and the teaching of our Lord Jesus Christ. The third image is that he learns to acknowledge our Lord’s suffering and his death out of great love. These are the most useful images. For no person can ever grow to great things unless he has—

first wisely passed through these images.

Which are now the most noble <term>images</term> <note>original: "beelden" – refers to the mental representations or concepts used in meditation to understand divine truths.</note>? The first is that a person turns himself toward the high unions of the human and Divine natures. The second is toward the nobility and the richness of his own spirit or soul. The third is toward the worthy body of our Lord. These three images, well-observed, are the most noble images.

Which are the purest images? The first is that a person turns himself toward the holy Trinity of the three Persons. The second is that a person turns himself toward how the Son is eternally born from the Father and remains within; and how from them both the Holy Spirit, proceeding, also remains within. The third is that bottomless, essential, simple being of the Godhead. To contemplate these as far as one is able—those are the purest images.

Why shall one <term>give leave</term> <note>original: "oorlof geven" – a technical term in mystical literature meaning to dismiss, bid farewell to, or detach from something.</note> to all images? Because they are nothing but a path to the naked truth. If I am now to come to the naked truth, then I must give leave to the path and pass through all good images in the right <term>order</term> <note>original: "ordinantien"</note>, from the lowest to the middle and the highest, so that no truth escapes me. For this is one of the noblest works that a person can perform here: to walk intellectually <note>original: "vernufftelijck" – referring to the use of the higher intellect or spiritual reason.</note> among noble images.

This, then, is what perfected people possess—those who have completely died to all **self-seeking** and who stand in **essential truth** <note>original: "weselijcker waerheydt" — a central concept in Rhineland-Flemish mysticism referring to a truth that is not just known, but lived and integrated into one's very being.</note>, immovable and equanimous in all circumstances: in love, in sorrow, in having, in lacking, in living, and in dying. 

The sixth sign is that a person, standing thus in essential truth, is always turning inward into the hidden, heavenly, unknown **will of God**, and completely loses his own will therein, so that he becomes entirely **will-less** <note>original: "willeloos" — this does not mean a lack of agency, but a state of total surrender where the individual ego no longer dictates desires.</note>. He no longer desires either good or evil for himself; rather, he wills nothing at all, for he no longer possesses a will of his own. And there is no <term>counter-object</term> <note>original: "teghentworp" — an opposing goal or object that distracts the will from God.</note> for his will, and this is because he acknowledges the bare will of God in the **"now"** <note>original: "nu" — likely referring to the "eternal now," the mystical experience of God's presence outside of linear time.</note>. Therefore, he stands empty of all personal willing and lets God alone will. 

This is the highest union and the receiving of the human will into God's will. And all of this together finds its cause in the **suffering of Christ**, into which the person turns and washes himself of everything that is not God. In this great treasure that lies hidden in the suffering of our Lord, he is entirely bound to God, and thus he reaches the highest degree of **perfection**. ## The Epistle of Doctor John Tauler <note>John Tauler (c. 1300–1361) was a famous German Dominican mystic and theologian whose writings were highly influential in the Low Countries.</note> to his spiritual friends and children, which enlighten the heart and kindle it in the love of God.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

->How one shall live a spiritual life within a community.<-

In Christ Jesus and in his eternal love, greetings to all God-loving people who wish to serve God not only according to his commandments, but also according to his faithful twelve Evangelical counsels <term>Evangelical counsels: "Evangelische raeden," usually referring to the vows of poverty, chastity, and obedience, though Tauler here refers to an expanded list of twelve specific spiritual guidelines</term>. And especially those who live in holy gatherings <note>referring to monasteries or religious communities</note> or other "poor children" <note>a term for humble spiritual followers or those who have embraced spiritual poverty</note>, they shall observe with desire and follow these written teachings. By these means, they live for the honor of God and for their own salvation.

Dear children in Christ Jesus <note>original: "In Christo Jesu"</note>, all disorder of the inner and outer person is brought into order through the resignation <term>resignation: the Dutch "ghelaetenheyt" (akin to the German "Gelassenheit") refers to a state of surrendered detachment where one lets go of self-will to rely entirely on God</term> of oneself under God in all His judgments and permissions <note>referring to things God allows to happen, even if they seem difficult</note>. ## CHAPTER LXI.

### Concerning six points, to remain immovably united with God.

A person who wishes to be God's own <note>original: "Godts wil zijn" – meaning to belong to God or live according to His will</note> ought to observe six points; these are three outward and three inward. The first outward point is that his clothing be simple, and all his outward affairs should please no one but God alone. The second is that his words be short, necessary, and simple, and concern Divine matters. The third is that his whole life and his works—whatever he does—should be beyond reproach <note>original: "ghestraft" – literally "punished," here meaning rebuked or found lacking</note> by anyone.

The first inward teaching is this: that his thoughts be clear and heavenly. The second is that God alone be sought in all his intentions <note>original: "meyninghe" – refers to one's inner purpose or aim</note>. The third is that one must let go of all things for God’s sake—that is, that one be profoundly content with whatever happens to him, so that he remains immovably peaceful, just as water stands still when the wind does not blow upon it. In this way, his inner ground <term>ground (gront): the mystical "core" or deepest part of the soul, which must be still to reflect God</term> shall remain still and immovable. Just as a person cannot see himself in the water as long as it flows and is disturbed, so too the clear, simple Good that is God Himself can ne-

### Another short teaching.

All the manifold <term>exercises (oeffeninghen): spiritual practices or disciplines</term> of the book—indeed, all that one may write concerning a godly life—are together obtained in this way: in <term>detachment (afghescheydenheyt): the spiritual state of being withdrawn from worldly attachments</term> from all created, perishable things; in humble <term>resignation (ghelaetenheyt): the act of surrendering one's will and desires to God</term>; in inner emptiness; and in embracing God alone through faith and love in the <term>naked ground (blooten gront): the deepest, most essential part of the soul where it meets God</term> of our souls. We are to hide ourselves—with our spirit, soul, body, heart, and senses—in His Holy humanity, and to become like the same through living <term>imitation (naervolghinghe): the active following of Christ's example</term>; and through her merit <note>The author uses "her" because "Humanity" (menscheydt) is a feminine noun in the original Dutch.</note> to always cling to His Divinity. Whoever does this fulfills all that is written above. And he is strengthened and worked upon by God, and always maintains a free <term>inwardness (inkeer): the ability to turn one's focus away from the world and back into the soul</term>, and all his works become divine through this, and he himself as well; so that he knows the living truth of Holy <term>Scripture (Schriftuere)</term>, as it shines in all pure hearts in pursuing perfection.

O all people, awake from the sleep of your sins and manifold failings, and prepare yourselves by the amendment of your life against the great, miserable distress and anxiety that shall come upon you and meet you at your last end—before the strict <note>original: "strange" — in this context meaning severe or rigorous rather than unusual.</note> judgment of God—at the hands of the hellish enemies. The judge stands before the door and is ready to reward you according to your merits. Oh, learn while you have time and can still find God, to turn from all sins to God, and take heed of his grace. For in the final distress, it will stand much more perilously for many people who deceive themselves than they can now imagine. So that you may firmly establish yourselves in the fear of the Lord (which is the beginning of all wisdom), I will faithfully explain to you a little regarding the distinction of God's judgments which souls encounter when they depart from the body—as much as can be understood with the senses and the intellect, just as God has revealed to his secret friends <term>original: "heymelijcke vrienden" — likely referring to the "Friends of God" (Gottesfreunde), a 14th-century mystical movement in the Low Countries and Germany that emphasized a personal, inner union with God.</term>.

# HISTORY
## And life of the venerable and enlightened Doctor
# JOHN TAULER,
### Who in Cologne was converted from his vain life to a Holy life.

In the year written after Christ’s birth, one thousand three hundred forty / there was a master of the Holy Scriptures <note>original: *meester der Heyligher Schriftueren*; likely referring to a Doctor of Divinity, a high academic and ecclesiastical rank.</note> in a city / who often preached / and people also heard him gladly / and his teachings were spoken of for many miles around. A layman, rich in grace, heard of this / and was admonished three times in his sleep that he should go to the city where this master was / and should hear him preach. Now the city was in another land, a good thirty miles from his own city. Then the man thought: I will go there / and understand what God wishes to work there. He arrived in the city / and heard the Master’s sermons <note>original: *Predicatien*</note> five times. Then God gave this man to understand that the master was a good, meek / and kind-hearted man by nature / and had a good understanding of scripture / but he was <note>The text ends mid-word with "ver-". ### THE LIFE

The Golden A.B.C. which this man gave to the Doctor to learn / and to improve his life thereafter.

**A.** **A**t a good life you shall begin with diligence / manfully / and not childishly. <note>The layman challenges the learned Doctor to approach his spiritual rebirth with the grit of an adult, rather than the fickle nature of a child.</note>
**B.** **B**adness you shall leave / and do good with a deliberate spirit / steadfastly.
**C.** **C**ome to maintain a proper / and tempered **moderation** <term>middelmaeticheyt: the virtue of the "middle way," avoiding extremes in both worldly indulgence and prideful, excessive asceticism</term>.
**D.** **D**o your best to learn to carry yourself inwardly and outwardly in quiet / and **humility** <term>oodtmoet: a central theme in Tauler’s thought, meaning to make oneself small or "nothing" before God</term>.
**E.** **E**go and **own-will** <term>eyghen wille: the selfish desires and personal attachments that mystics believed must be "killed" or renounced to allow God to act within the soul</term> you must root out and thoroughly renounce for God’s sake / so that you may remain united with God / and God with you.
**F.** **F**inely / bravely / and firmly you shall persevere in God.
**G.** **G**enerously / and diligently you shall be submissive with joy / and show yourself willing without grumbling.
**H.** **H**ither / nor thither shall you look back / toward the world or any **creatures** <term>creaturen: in mystical theology, this refers to any created thing—people, status, or material goods—that might distract the soul from the Creator</term> / nor toward their works.

It happened before that year passed / that the Master <note>Johannes Tauler, who held a prestigious Doctorate in Theology.</note> was held in such low esteem in the monastery / and all his close friends / and his spiritual children <note>Those who sought him for confession and spiritual advice.</note> all ran from him / just as if they had never seen him before. Now when the Master had suffered thus for a good two years in great temptation <note>original: "aenvechtinge." In the context of 14th-century mysticism, this refers to a period of intense spiritual trial, doubt, or "darkness of the soul."</note>, and in great contempt from all his friends, and in great poverty—so much so that he had to pawn a portion of his books—and he also fell into a great sickness of his body, yet he had conducted himself in great humility.

Because of this, all his natural strengths became so weak that at that time he could not go to <term>Matins: the first prayer service of the liturgical day, typically held in the middle of the night or very early morning</term>. # APPROVAL <note>original: *Approbatio*; an official statement from the Church certifying that the book contains no heresy</note>.

*The desires of pious minds will be satisfied if the marrow of the soul <note>original: medulla animæ; a metaphor for the essential spiritual core of a person’s teachings</note> of*
**JOHANNES TAULER** *is reprinted. Done*
*November 18, 1633.*

-> Gaspar Estrix, Censor of books and Parish Priest <-
-> of Antwerp. <-

---

# PRIVILEGE <note>original: *Privilegie*; a form of early copyright granted by the sovereign to a specific printer</note>.

PHilip, by the grace of God King of
Castile, of Aragon, of Leon, of both the Si-
cilies, etc. Archduke of Austria,
Duke of Burgundy, of Lorraine, of Brabant,
etc. Count of Habsburg, of Flanders, of
Artois, etc. Count Palatine of Hainaut, of Holland,
of Zeeland, etc. has consented and per-
mitted, and by this document consents and permits,
Hendrick Aertssens, sworn book printer, the right to
print *The Marrow of Souls*, composed by
the very enlightened Doctor **JOHANNES TAULER**,
and translated into Dutch by Lord Anthonis van Hemert. For-
bidding all other book printers or book sel-
lers from reprinting the same in whole or in part, or
bringing or selling copies printed elsewhere into
these Lands, upon the forfeiture of the said books, and
other penalties, as is more fully detailed in the letters patent
given at Brussels, in the year 1633, the
20th of November.

-> By the King in his Council. <-

-> Signed <-

-> Steenhuyse. <-
